statement: CRS describes the maximum additional child tax credit (the refundable portion) as $1,700 per child for 2025, adjusted for inflation, and says the 2025 law makes the TCJA credit changes permanent and sets the credit at $2,200 per child, adjusted for inflation.

context: Primary law, section 70104(b), replacing section 24(h)(7). Before the law only the child needed an SSN; the new rule excludes citizen children with SSNs whose parents have only ITINs. Existing register entry on the same rule: EV-HOU-405 (from IRS Schedule 8812 instructions).

statement: The refundable part of the child tax credit is 15 percent of earned income above $2,500: the code applies 15 percent to earnings above $3,000 and then substitutes $2,500 for $3,000.
anchor: (i) 15 percent of so much of the taxpayer's earned income (within the meaning of section 32) which is taken into account in computing taxable income for the taxable year as exceeds $3,000, or
Subsection (d)(1)(B)(i) shall be applied by substituting "$2,500" for "$3,000".
context: U.S. Code, 2024 edition (before P.L. 119-21). Section 70104 amends section 24(h)(1) to remove the end date, so section 24(h)(6) stays in force with no end date; it does not amend section 24(d). The credit is therefore zero for a family with no income tax liability and under $2,500 of earnings (see EV-SEC-011).

statement: The child tax credit phases out by $50 for each $1,000 of modified adjusted gross income above $400,000 for a joint return and $200,000 for any other return.
anchor: reduced (but not below zero) by $50 for each $1,000 (or fraction thereof) by which the taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income exceeds the threshold amount.
the threshold amount shall be $400,000 in the case of a joint return ($200,000 in any other case).
context: U.S. Code, 2024 edition. Permanence rests on section 70104(a), which strikes the end date in section 24(h)(1); CRS R48611 (EV-SEC-004 source) states it: "increased the income limits to $200,000 for single filers and $400,000 for married couples filing jointly". The $50 per $1,000 is a 5 percent phase-out rate.

statement: CRS says the TCJA created a $500 nonrefundable credit, not adjusted for inflation, for dependents who are not qualifying children, and that the 2025 law makes the TCJA changes permanent.

context: CRS description of enacted law. Statute: section 24(h)(4)(A) (U.S. Code 2024 edition, SRC-3607). The credit is the only credit open to a child with an ITIN rather than an SSN (CBPP, SRC-3635, says so); a citizen child of parents with only ITINs may be claimed for it as a dependent.

statement: Section 70204 creates Trump accounts (new section 530A) and a Trump Accounts Contribution Pilot Program under which an election by the parent treats an eligible child as paying $1,000 of tax, which is refunded to the child's Trump account, for a qualifying child born after December 31, 2024 and before January 1, 2029.

context: Primary law. CRS (R48611, SRC-3011) adds that the beneficiary must be a U.S. citizen with a work-authorized SSN and that the account invests in a diversified U.S. stock index fund; contributions are capped at $5,000 a year. The $1,000 is a one-time deposit, not income support to the family.

statement: The 2025 law creates a deduction of $6,000 for each taxpayer age 65 or older for 2025 through 2028, reduced by 6 percent of modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 on a joint return), for taxpayers with work-eligible Social Security numbers.
anchor: It also temporarily creates a new $6,000 deduction for taxpayers (and their spouses, if married filing jointly) who are age 65 or older, from 2025 through 2028.
This amount is reduced by 6% of a taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 for those married filing jointly).
context: CRS description of enacted law (section 70103). Temporary: it ends after tax year 2028, before the January 2029 baseline date for the new administration. It is a deduction, so it is worth nothing to a household that owes no income tax.

statement: The Tax Policy Center estimated that in 2025, 17 million children under 17, one in four, would receive less than the full child tax credit because their parents earn too little; about 2 million get nothing because they earn under $2,500 and owe no tax.
anchor: But in 2025, the Tax Policy Center estimates that 17 million children under the age of 17—or one in four—will receive less than the full value of the credit because their parents earn too little.
Families that do not owe federal income taxes and earn less than $2,500 receive no CTC. That’s about 2 million children
locator: opening paragraphs; section on who receives the full value
context: Tax Policy Center (Urban-Brookings, nonpartisan), December 10, 2024: microsimulation for 2025 under the then-current $2,000 credit, before the 2025 law. The 17 million is the share below the $2,000 maximum; the later TPC post (EV-SEC-012) says the same count at $2,200.

statement: In June 2026 the Tax Policy Center restated that roughly 17 million children live in families that do not receive the full $2,200 per child because their families' earnings are too low.
anchor: roughly 17 million children live in families that do not receive the full $2,200 per child CTC because their families’ earnings are too low

The count differs from Columbia's 19 million (EV-SEC-013) in method: Columbia adds about two million moderate-income children newly short of a larger maximum.

statement: Columbia's Center on Poverty and Social Policy estimated that in 2025 more than 1 in 4 children (28%) under age 17, 19 million, would be ineligible for the full child tax credit under the 2025 law because family income is not high enough; a two-parent, two-child family needs at least $41,500.
anchor: more than 1 in 4 children (28%) under age 17 will be ineligible for the full Child Tax Credit under OBBBA because their family income is not high enough to qualify

This represents 19 million children left behind: 17 million children previously ineligible for the full credit who see no gains under OBBBA and remain ineligible for the full credit plus roughly two million children in moderate-income families newly ineligible for the full credit.
a two-parent family with two children will need a minimum of $41,500 in income to be eligible for the full credit under OBBBA
context: Columbia University Center on Poverty and Social Policy, August 6, 2025, brief by Collyer, Yera, Curran, Harris and Wimer; simulation on Census survey data of the law as signed; the center advocates a more fully refundable credit. Higher than TPC's 17 million (EV-SEC-012) because it counts the children whose families fall short of the larger $2,200 maximum.

statement: CBO estimated that the SNAP work-requirement changes reduce participation by roughly 2.4 million people in an average month over 2025-2034, including about 800,000 able-bodied adults through age 64 without dependent children and 300,000 adults 18 to 64 living with a child 14 or older.
anchor: CBO estimates that together those provisions will reduce participation in SNAP by roughly 2.4 million people in an average month over the 2025-2034 period.

anchor:
All mandatory state leave insurance programs are financed through payroll contributions, with
some variation in how contributions are allocated between employers and employees. Program

statement: Using March CPS data from 1999-2010, Rossin-Slater, Ruhm and Waldfogel found California's program doubled use of maternity leave from an average of around 3 to 6 weeks and increased the usual weekly work hours of employed mothers of one-to-three-year-olds by 10 to 17%.

paid family leave led to 10 to 17% increases in usual weekly work hours for employed mothers
March Current Population Survey data from 1999–2010
context: Peer reviewed (JPAM 2013); difference-in-differences with comparison groups of older-child mothers, childless women and other states; tried in California, 2004 program (six weeks at 55%). The 2011 NBER working paper reported 6 to 9% for hours and "three to six or seven weeks"; the published 10 to 17% is the later, stronger statement. The authors call the labor market evidence "more equivocal." Co-authored by Ruhm, who also wrote the Baum study.

statement: Baum and Ruhm found, using a national youth survey cohort, that California's program raised leave use by almost five weeks for the average covered mother and two to three days for the father, and was associated with higher work and employment probabilities for mothers nine to 12 months after birth.

higher work and employment probabilities for mothers nine to 12 months after birth
context: Peer reviewed (JPAM 2016); difference-in-differences against control states, NLSY-97 cohort (small sample); tried in California. Shares an author (Ruhm) with the Rossin-Slater study, so not independent of it.

statement: Using IRS and SSA tax data and a regression discontinuity in time, Bailey, Byker, Patel and Ramnath found no evidence that California's 2004 Paid Family Leave Act increased women's employment, earnings or childbearing, and found it reduced employment and earnings of first-time mothers roughly a decade after birth.
anchor: effects of California’s 2004 Paid Family Leave Act (CPFL)
We find no evidence that CPFL increased employment, boosted earnings, or encouraged childbearing
For first-time mothers, we find that CPFL reduced employment and earnings roughly a decade after they gave birth.
context: NBER working paper 26416 (2019, revised January 2024), published in AEJ: Economic Policy 2025; compares mothers giving birth just after May 20, 2004, who could take paid leave consecutively after disability leave, with those just before; tried in California only. CONTESTS the positive findings above. The brief recalled larger 2019-version figures (about 7% fewer employed, 8% lower earnings); the revised abstract quotes no percentages, and a paragraph of the paper says no negative effects for mothers who already had children. Short-run effects were not negative. Identifies effects of the sharp rise in weeks at the 2004 launch, six weeks at 55%.

statement: Jones and Wilcher found that California's paid family leave decreased maternal labor force detachment by 5 percentage points, with impacts still significantly different from zero up to nine years later, and similar effects in New Jersey, Rhode Island and New York.

Impacts on detachment remain significantly different from zero up to nine years later.

context: Peer reviewed (Labour Economics, April 2024); difference-in-differences on survey data around the 2004 California launch, with effects largest among women with bachelor's degrees; tried in California, then checked in three other states. CONTESTS Bailey et al. on long-run outcomes (different data: survey participation, not tax records).

statement: The 2025 law's new $6,000 deduction for people age 65 or older runs from 2025 through 2028 and is reduced by 6% of modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 for joint filers).
anchor: It also temporarily creates a new $6,000 deduction for taxpayers (and their spouses, if married filing jointly) who are age 65 or older, from 2025 through 2028. This amount is reduced by 6% of a taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income above $75,000 ($150,000 for those married filing jointly).
context: CRS (nonpartisan) description of section 70103 of P.L. 119-21. The deduction ends after tax year 2028, so it is not in force in 2029 unless extended. It adds a 6 percent phase-out layer for older filers in its range.

context: The 2014 reauthorization of the CCDBG (Obama administration; bipartisan). The "graduated phaseout" requirement is a continued-assistance rule; it does not require any particular copayment slope. HHS's May 2026 final rule rescinded the 7 percent copayment cap (EV-CAR-510).

statement: CCDF eligibility requires a child to live with a family whose income does not exceed 85 percent of state median income, based on the most recent Census Bureau data, for a family of the same size.
anchor: (2)(i) Reside with a family whose income does not exceed 85 percent of the State's median income (SMI), which must be based on the most recent SMI data that is published by the Bureau of the Census, for a family of the same size; and
context: 45 CFR 98.20(a)(2)(i) (eCFR, November 2026). The 85 percent is a federal ceiling; states set lower entry lines and most serve only a fraction of eligible families (EV-SEC-563 for Colorado).

statement: There are no federal rules on the amount of TANF cash benefits; states alone determine them, and a family with other income often receives a reduced benefit.
anchor: There are no federal rules that help determine the amount of TANF cash benefits paid to a family.
Benefit amounts are determined solely by the states.
Families with income other than TANF often are paid a reduced benefit.
context: CRS (nonpartisan), 2024 edition of the TANF FAQ report. Benefit data in the report are from July 2022 (a family of two received from $915 a month in New Hampshire to $162 in Arkansas). TANF phase-out rules (earned income disregards) vary by state; the Urban Institute's Welfare Rules Database is the state-by-state source (not saved; evidence still needed).

statement: ASPE lists SNAP, the National School Lunch Program, LIHEAP, Head Start and the Children's Health Insurance Program among programs using the poverty guidelines or multiples of them (for instance 125 or 185 percent), and says TANF, SSI and the earned income credit do not use them.
anchor: Programs using the guidelines (or percentage multiples of the guidelines — for instance, 125 percent or 185 percent of the guidelines) in determining eligibility include Head Start, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the National School Lunch Program, the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, and the Children’s Health Insurance Program.

Note that in general, cash public assistance programs (Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Supplemental Security Income) do NOT use the poverty guidelines in determining eligibility. The Earned Income Tax Credit program also does NOT use the poverty guidelines to determine eligibility.
context: HHS ASPE, second Trump administration, plain description. Housing uses area median income (EV-SEC-512), CCDF state median income (EV-SEC-530), the tax credits tax filing units.

statement: Under the tax code's refund-disregard rule any refund, or advance payment of a refundable credit, made to an individual under the tax code is not income, and not a resource for 12 months, in determining eligibility or benefit amounts under any federal program or any state or local program financed in whole or in part with federal funds.
anchor: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any refund (or advance payment with respect to a refundable credit) made to any individual under this title shall not be taken into account as income, and shall not be taken into account as resources for a period of 12 months from receipt, for purposes of determining the eligibility of such individual (or any other individual) for benefits or assistance (or the amount or extent of benefits or assistance) under any Federal program or under any State or local program financed in whole or in part with Federal funds.
context: The statute (2024 edition). It is why a refundable child benefit paid through the tax system does not raise rent or reduce SNAP (dossiers/shared-rules.md, rule 1). A benefit paid outside the tax code has no such protection unless its own statute says so.

statement: CRS states that there is no uniform definition of modified adjusted gross income; the term has different definitions depending on the purpose for which it is being calculated.
anchor: There is no uniform definition of MAGI; rather, the term has different definitions depending on the purpose for which it is being calculated.
context: CRS (nonpartisan), R43861 (2016). Older report; the tax-code definitions it compares have been amended since (for example for the senior deduction, EV-SEC-505, which defines its own MAGI).

statement: CRS reported that Supplemental Security Income and Veterans Affairs benefits use income definitions which include most sources of income, taxable and nontaxable, while Medicaid and the premium credit use a tax-based MAGI definition.
anchor: which include most sources of income, taxable and nontaxable, when determining eligibility.
most other low-income programs include other types of income (e.g., nontaxable pensions) and asset holdings that are also exc
locator: Definitions of Income Used in Selected Low-Income Programs
context: CRS (nonpartisan), R41997 (2011-2013 versions). Only a 2011-2013 CRS comparison table was found; no current CRS or GAO report comparing income definitions across federal programs was found (evidence still needed). Its second quotation is cut off at the saved text's own line wrap.

statement: CBO estimated that in 2016, counting federal payroll taxes, state income taxes and the phase-out of SNAP and cost-sharing subsidies, only 16 percent of low- and moderate-income taxpayers would face a marginal tax rate between 10 and 19 percent and 78 percent a higher rate, against 48 percent and 23 percent under the federal income tax alone; more than half would face 20 to 39 percent.
anchor: CBO estimates that in 2016, about 48 percent of low- and moderate-income taxpayers under age 65 with earnings will face a marginal tax rate between 10 percent and 19 percent under the federal income tax system, and 23 percent will face a higher rate
Only 16 percent of taxpayers will face marginal tax rates between 10 percent and 19 percent, and 78 percent will face higher rates.
More than half will face marginal tax rates between 20 percent and 39 percent.
context: CBO (nonpartisan), November 2015; tax-return simulation of workers under 450 percent of poverty. It includes SNAP and the ACA cost-sharing subsidies but not housing assistance or TANF, so it understates the stack for assisted families. It does not report the share above 50 or 60 percent in the text read; the distribution above 50 percent, and the CBO 2012 report (pub. 43709), are evidence still needed.

statement: CBO's hypothetical single parent with one child in Pennsylvania faced marginal tax rates averaging 75 percent over a narrow range of income (115 to 126 percent of poverty), from the combined phase-out of the earned income credit and SNAP, the 10 percent income tax bracket and the 15.3 percent payroll tax.
anchor: The combination of the phaseout of the EITC and SNAP benefits, the 10 percent federal income tax bracket, and the 15.3 percent federal payroll tax causes a sharp increase in marginal tax rates, which average 75 percent over a narrow range of income (from 115 percent to 126 percent of the FPL).
context: CBO (nonpartisan), November 2015; a stylized family receiving TANF, SNAP, Medicaid/CHIP and cost-sharing subsidies, 2016 law (pre-2017 tax law, ACA 400 percent cliff). CBO says it "is not indicative of the distribution". Pennsylvania chosen as typical of state income taxes.

statement: CBO estimated that 62 percent of lower-income families did not receive means-tested transfers in 2013, and of those who did, most participated in only one program.
anchor: An estimated 62 percent of lower-income families did not receive those means-tested transfers in 2013, either because they did not meet additional nonfinancial requirements or because they were eligible but did not apply for benefits. Of those who received transfers, most participated in only one program.
context: CBO (nonpartisan), November 2015, from the 2014 CPS ASEC; transfers were TANF, SNAP, Medicaid, CHIP and cost-sharing subsidies. This is why CBO's average (31 percent, EV-HOU-401) is far below the stacked examples.

context: HHS ASPE (Chien and Macartney), March 2019, first Trump administration; TRIM3 microsimulation on the 2015 CPS ASEC; a $2,000 earnings increase from federal and state taxes and transfers. Agency analysis, treated with the usual skepticism; the series page defines a cliff as a benefit reduction equal to or larger than the earnings increase.

statement: Maag, Steuerle, Chakravarti and Quakenbush found that a single parent with two children whose wages rise from the poverty level to 150 percent of poverty can face a marginal tax rate between 26.6 percent and over 100 percent depending on the state, and that the rate varies sharply with earnings pattern and program participation.
anchor: A single parent with two children who increases her wages from poverty-level to 150 percent of poverty-level can face a tax rate between 26.6 percent and over 100 percent, depending on which state she lives in.
This paper shows how sensitive marginal tax rates are to assumptions about state of residence, earning patterns, and program participation.
context: Urban Institute and Tax Policy Center researchers; peer reviewed (National Tax Journal 65(4), December 2012); a simulation of a family across states under 2012 law. Authors warn the rates may overstate what families face because they assume income is earned evenly through the year.

statement: Using the 2019 Survey of Consumer Finances and a life-cycle model, Altig and co-authors found that over half of working-age Americans face lifetime marginal net tax rates above 40 percent, one in four households in the bottom lifetime resource quintile above 50 percent, and one in ten above 70 percent.
anchor: We use TFA in conjunction with the 2019 Survey of Consumer Finances to calculate Americans’ remaining lifetime marginal net tax rates (LMTR).
Over half of working-age Americans face LMTRs exceeding 40 percent. One in four households in the bottom lifetime resource quintile face LMTRs above 50 percent. One in ten face rates above 70 percent
context: NBER working paper 27164 (2020, revised 2023); not peer reviewed. Funded by the Sloan Foundation, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta and the Goodman Institute; Kotlikoff owns the firm whose engine is used (disclosed). Model-based, includes lifetime effects (benefits and taxes over the life cycle), so not directly comparable with current-year rates.

statement: In the Atlanta Fed's illustration of a hypothetical single mother with two children in Clarke County, Georgia, moving from concessions worker to certified nursing assistant lowers net resources by more than $11,000 over three years, and from nursing assistant to licensed practical nurse by more than $35,000, which the page attributes to reduced work hours while in school and benefits cliffs; over a lifetime both moves pay.
anchor: The chart above demonstrates an example of benefits cliffs for a hypothetical single mother with two children who lives in Clarke County, Georgia.
Leia's cumulatively experiences a decline of more than $11,000.
Leia would suffer a loss of net financial resources exceeding $35,000 during the first three years of the transition.
These declines are the results of reduced work hours while in school and the prevalence of benefits cliffs.
When resources are calculated over a lifetime, however, both scenarios would deliver a positive return
locator: What Are Benefits Cliffs?, Leia example
context: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta (central-bank research arm; promotes its CLIFF tools), undated web page; a worked example from its Policy Rules Database/CLIFF model, not a measured sample. The page does not break the loss down by program; the Ilin and Sanchez paper on mitigating cliffs was not found (evidence still needed).

statement: PolicyEngine simulated a Texas couple's premium tax credit: at 400% of poverty they are ineligible under the law after the enhanced credits expire, and would gain $2,899 a year had the enhanced credits been extended, which produces an infinite marginal rate at the cliff.
anchor: the Texas couple would gain $2,899 in annual credits at 400% FPL
a positive infinite MTR at 400% FPL under current law, where they become ineligible for the PTC
context: PolicyEngine (nonprofit open-source microsimulation), September 30, 2025, before the enhanced credits expired; archetype households, 2026 values. An "infinite" rate is the arithmetic of a cliff (loss of credit over a $1 rise). Not independently validated here.

statement: Under SSDI rules in 2019, beneficiaries who engaged in substantial gainful activity (earnings of $1,220 a month for most) for more than a year had their entire benefit suspended, creating a "cash cliff".
anchor: Under current SSDI rules, when beneficiaries engage in substantial gainful activity (SGA—defined as earnings of $1,220 per month for most SSDI beneficiaries) for more than a year, SSA suspends their entire benefit payment. This rule creates a “cash cliff” at the SGA threshold
context: Abt Global brief on the SSA-funded BOND trial, 2019; a description of the rule then in force, not a result. The 2026 amount is $1,690 (EV-SEC-525).

statement: In BOND, a randomized test run for SSA of a $1-for-$2 benefit offset on SSDI earnings above the annual equivalent of the substantial gainful activity amount, the evaluation found no statistically significant impact on average earnings in either stage, though the offset raised the share of beneficiaries with earnings above that amount by 7 percent in Stage 1 and 23 percent in Stage 2.
anchor: BOND tested a $1 for $2 benefit offset applied to annual earnings above the BOND Yearly Amount (BYA)

The evaluation found no statistically significant evidence of an impact of the benefit offset policy on average earnings either in the nationally representative Stage 1 sample or in the Stage 2 sample of volunteers.
the evaluation finds evidence in both stages that the benefit offset increased the share of beneficiaries with earnings above BYA—by 7 percent in Stage 1 and by 23 percent in Stage 2
context: Randomized trial run for SSA by Abt Associates with Mathematica; Stage 1 randomized 968,530 SSDI beneficiaries (2011 to 2015), Stage 2 12,744 volunteers; Abt brief of 2019 on the 2018 final report. The 7 and 23 percent are relative increases over the control mean, not percentage points.

statement: BOND also found the offset raised average SSDI benefits by $143 a year in Stage 1, and that 3.6 percent of the Stage 1 treatment group earned enough to trigger the offset in at least one year, against about 15 percent of the treatment groups in the volunteer sample.
anchor: In the nationally representative Stage 1 sample, the benefit offset increased average SSDI benefits by $143 per year (or about $12 per month) during the five year period.
Of the Stage 1 sample, 3.6 percent of the treatment group earned enough to trigger the offset, resulting in a reduction in their benefits, in at least one year during the follow-up period
About 15 percent of the treatment groups earned enough to trigger partial benefit payments in any year during the follow-up period
context: Same trial as EV-SEC-546. Two forces raised benefits: partial benefits to people who already earned above the line, and some of them cutting earnings. Most who triggered the offset would have earned that much anyway.

statement: SSA's BOND page reports that use of the benefit offset was modest, enhanced counseling had the same effect as regular counseling, and a benefit-cost analysis showed the total cost of the offset exceeded its total benefit.
anchor: The use of the benefit offset was modest, and enhanced counseling services had the same effect as regular counseling services. A benefit-cost analysis showed that the total cost of the benefit offset exceeded its total benefit.
context: SSA (second Trump administration, 2026 summary page) of the trial it commissioned. Same trial as the Abt brief, so corroboration of method but from a different publisher; the page's summary is the agency's.

statement: Saez found clear bunching around the first kink of the earned income credit concentrated solely among the self-employed, and no bunching at any other kink of the income tax schedule apart from the first bracket threshold.
anchor: We find clear evidence of bunching around the first kink point of the Earned Income Tax Credit but concentrated solely among the self-employed.
We find evidence of bunching at the threshold of the first income tax bracket where tax liability starts but no evidence of bunching at any other kink point.
context: Peer reviewed (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy, August 2010); US tax-return data; observational, not experimental. Bunching at a kink is evidence about reported income, which can reflect reporting rather than hours worked.

statement: Census Bureau researchers found that bunching around the poverty-line notch where premium tax credits start, in states that did not expand Medicaid, occurs only among filers with self-employment income, and found no evidence that wage and salary workers adjust their labor supply in response to the new subsidy.
anchor: bunching occurs only among ﬁlers with self-employment income.

no evidence that wage and salary workers adjust their labor supply in response to increased availability
of directly purchased health insurance.
context: Kucko, Rinz and Solow, Census CARRA working paper 2017-07; not peer reviewed; tax records for the universe of returns, 2014 onward. The "100 percent" appears in the abstract's description of the notch.

statement: Using IRS data, Heim and co-authors found bunching of taxpayer incomes below 400% of poverty in 2014 that is only apparent among marketplace purchasers who could get the subsidy, among both self-employed and wage and salary workers, and primarily through increased IRA contributions.
anchor: We find a significant amount of bunching below 400% FPL in 2014 that is only apparent among those who purchased insurance from a marketplace
We see evidence of bunching at the cliff both among the self-employed and among wage and salary workers.
the bunching appears to primarily have been driven by increases in contributions to IRA accounts
context: Conference abstract (ASHEcon 2016) by Treasury-affiliated and Indiana University authors; the paper was later published in the Journal of Health Economics (2020), where the authors describe the overall amount of bunching as modest. IRS tax returns 2013 and 2014 (a difference-in-differences against 2013, when no subsidy existed). Shares authors with EV-SEC-552.

statement: Treasury-affiliated researchers estimated that around 85,000 taxpayers likely to have bought exchange insurance had income between 390% and 410% of poverty; close to 40% of them faced a cliff smaller than $100, though over 30% faced one above $3000.
anchor: We also estimate that around 85,000 taxpayers who were likely to have purchased insurance in an exchange had MAGI between 390% and 410% of FPL.
Close to 40% of these will face a cliff smaller than $100, though over 30% will face a cliff in excess of $3000.
context: National Tax Association proceedings, October 2014; tax data for 2011-2012 matched to exchange premiums, simulating 2014 rules; authors shared with EV-SEC-551. The authors note a larger cliff would exist if premiums rise faster than incomes. Under the 2026 schedule the credit is larger than in 2014 for many (premiums have risen), so cliff sizes are likely bigger now (judgment, not measured).

statement: Moffitt records that the AFDC benefit-reduction rate was 100 percent from 1935 to the 1967 Social Security Amendments, which lowered it to 67 percent, and that the 1981 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act raised it back to 100 percent.
anchor: From 1935, when the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program was enacted, to the 1967 Social Security Amendments, the tax rate in the program was 100 percent-that is, benefits were reduced by one dollar for every extra dollar earned. With the 1967 Amendments, Congress lowered the tax rate to 67 percent
Welfare reform was finally achieved in 1981 when the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (OBRA) was enacted.
But OBRA increased the tax rate back to 100 percent, the level prevailing prior to 1967.
context: Peer-reviewed conference paper (American Economic Review Papers and Proceedings, 1986) by Robert Moffitt. A historical account of the "30 and a third" disregard the 1967 amendments created and the 1981 law removed.

statement: Moffitt and Wolf found that the 1981 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act hit working AFDC recipients hard, raising the implicit tax rate in the program to 78 percent, mainly by eliminating the "30-and-one-third" deduction.
anchor: The 1981 Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (OBRA) altered the Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) program in important ways
We find that working recipients were very hard hit and that the "tax rate" implicit in the program rose to 78 percent.
the elimination of the "30-and-one-third" deduction was most important in raising the tax rate.
context: Peer reviewed (Social Service Review, June 1987); data on AFDC recipients active just before the 1981 law; simulates the effect on the benefit formula, not on observed hours. Shares an author with EV-SEC-553, so not independent corroboration of it. The paper measures the incentive change; the labor-supply effect is Moffitt's econometric estimate in EV-SEC-553's source (not quoted here).

statement: In November 2021 the UK government cut the Universal Credit taper rate from 63% to 55% and raised work allowances by £500 a year.
anchor: Work allowances, the amount a claimant can earn before their Universal Credit is reduced, will increase by £500 per year from today
the taper rate, the amount that a person’s Universal Credit is reduced by when their earnings are more than their work allowance, will drop from 63% to 55%.
context: UK Department for Work and Pensions press release, November 24, 2021 (Conservative government). Universal Credit replaced six means-tested benefits (Jobseeker's Allowance, Income Support, Housing Benefit, Employment and Support Allowance, Working Tax Credit, Child Tax Credit) with one payment and one taper. The taper applies to net earnings above a work allowance for households with a child or limited capability for work; others have none.

statement: The UK National Audit Office concluded in 2018 that Universal Credit was not value for money then and its future value for money was unproven, and that it doubted the Department could ever measure whether the aim of increasing employment had been achieved.
anchor: cause us to conclude that the project is not value for money now, and that its future value for money is unproven.
Both we, and the Department, doubt it will ever be possible for the Department to measure whether the economic goal of increasing employment has been achieved.
context: UK National Audit Office (independent public auditor), June 2018; a value-for-money audit of the rollout (delivery, costs, claimant hardship), not of the taper design. The five-week wait for a first payment and the effect of the 63 to 55 percent cut on work are not covered here (an IFS or Resolution Foundation analysis is evidence still needed).

statement: For the Canada Child Benefit payments of July 2026 onward, the benefit is reduced by 7% of adjusted family net income between $38,237 and $82,847 for one child, 13.5% for two, 19% for three and 23% for four or more; above $82,847 the reduction is a fixed amount plus 3.2% of income above that line for one child.
anchor: These amounts start being reduced when the adjusted family net income (AFNI) is over $38,237.
the reduction is 7% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
the reduction is 13.5% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
the reduction is 19% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
the reduction is 23% of the amount of AFNI greater than $38,237 up to $82,847
for income greater than $82,847, the reduction is $3,123 plus 3.2% of AFNI greater than $82,847

context: Canada Revenue Agency (Canadian federal government), publication T4114 for the July 2026 to June 2027 payment year. The rates rise with the number of children, so the marginal rate is a function of family size; the phase-out is a single smooth schedule on one income measure.

statement: Canada Child Benefit entitlement is based on adjusted family net income for the calendar year before the benefit year, which in most cases equals net income on the tax return (the sum of both spouses' in a two-parent family).
anchor: In most cases, the AFNI is equal to the parent's net income as reported on the tax return in a one-parent family and to the sum of both spouses/common-law partners' net income in a two-parent family.
the CCB entitlement based on the adjusted family net income (AFNI) for the calendar year before the beginning of the benefit year
context: Department of Finance Canada, Report on Federal Tax Expenditures 2026. One income test from the tax return, run once a year, with payment monthly. Contrast with US programs that each re-verify income on their own cycle.

statement: Australia's Family Tax Benefit Part A is reduced by 20 cents per dollar of family adjusted taxable income over $69,131 (down to a base rate) and by 30 cents per dollar over $123,078 until it reaches nil.
anchor: This test reduces your FTB Part A by 20 cents for each dollar of income over $69,131.
We’ll reduce the rate of FTB Part A by 30 cents for each dollar of income over $123,078.
context: Services Australia (Australian federal government), page updated July 1, 2026. Income is "adjusted taxable income" from the tax system; payments can be reconciled after the tax return, which can cause overpayments.

statement: Under the transitional benefits alternative, a state that elects it freezes a household's SNAP allotment for up to 5 months after it leaves TANF, MOE or state-funded cash assistance, after adjusting for the loss of that income.
anchor: a State agency that has elected this option shall freeze the household's benefit allotment for up to 5 months after making an adjustment for the loss of TANF, MOE, or the SFCA.
context: 7 CFR 273.27(a) (eCFR, November 2026). State option.

statement: USDA's 2024 state options report counts 24 states and territories offering the transitional benefits alternative and 29 not offering it.
anchor: Benefits can be continued for up to 5 months at a level equal to the amount the household received prior to TANF termination
No TBA (29)
TBA (24)
context: USDA FNS, 16th State Options Report (June 2024, Biden administration); counts include Guam and the Virgin Islands. Later editions are not saved.

statement: GAO reported that under express lane eligibility a state Medicaid or CHIP agency may rely on another agency's findings (such as SNAP's income finding) even if that agency uses a different method, and that the option may be used only for children, not parents or other adults.
anchor: Under ELE, a state Medicaid or CHIP agency may rely on an Express Lane Agency’s findings even if the Express Lane Agency uses a different method than Medicaid or CHIP to derive those findings.
Under CHIPRA, the ELE option may only be used for Medicaid and CHIP eligibility determinations for children and cannot be used for parents or other adults.
context: GAO-13-178R (December 2012), nonpartisan legislative branch; describes the 2009 CHIPRA option. Children may be found eligible but not denied by ELE. Which states use it today, and its effects on enrollment, are not saved (CMS page blocks agents; evidence still needed).

statement: Colorado's Cliff Effect Pilot Program, authorized in 2012 in 15 counties, keeps families on child care assistance above the entry limit (statewide limit 165% of poverty; the program serves about 13% of eligible families); a 2019 evaluation presentation reported anecdotal evidence of greater economic mobility and recommended linking copay increases to income rises.
anchor: Authorized in 2012
15 counties
Statewide income eligibility: 165% FPL
Program only serves about 13% of eligible families
Families welcome assistance from CEPP, anecdotal evidence it enables greater economic mobility.
CEPP should link copay increases with household income increases
locator: slides: CCCAP Overview, Findings and Recommendations
context: Presentation by Colorado researchers to the National Governors Association, 2019; interviews and county data, no comparison group. The state pilot was the first of its kind; the evaluation says it is not well publicized. Later Colorado cliff measures (House Bill 1259 on TANF disregards) are not saved.
